channel_name: This Week in Startups · Jason Calacanis
video_title: Jason Mentors The Next Generation + Why AI Is Bad at Teaching (Aristotle Interview) | E2346
gist: Ask Jason call-in segment (career advice, $500K thought experiment, customer discovery 'dark arts', and AI doomerism as Frontier Lab marketing incl. Anthropic consulting religious scholars) followed by an interview with Aristotle CEO Sean Ready, who argues frontier models are getting worse at teaching and is building a voice AI tutor around 'next optimal pedagogical action' prediction, proprietary hand-graded tutoring data, and $50-$200/month tutoring-style pricing.

themes.theme: Aristotle: frontier models are getting worse at teaching

insights.claim: Aristotle CEO Sean Ready claims frontier AI models are getting worse, not better, at teaching, because the big labs bet that scaling general intelligence would scale pedagogical capacity and that bet has not paid off.
insights.speaker: Sean Ready (Aristotle)
insights.so_what: Suggests a durable gap for vertical edtech AI that general-purpose model improvements will not automatically close.
insights.quote: AI is actually not getting better at teaching, it's actually getting worse. The bet that the big labs have made is that scaling general intelligence is going to scale pedagogical capacity.

insights.claim: Sean Ready argues the behaviors produced by training for long-horizon reasoning, enterprise QA and coding (high verbosity, long answer-generation times) are counterproductive for tutoring, where the student must experience 'productive struggle' rather than delegate steps to the AI.
insights.speaker: Sean Ready (Aristotle)
insights.so_what: Identifies a structural misalignment between frontier-lab optimization targets and education outcomes.
insights.quote: the behaviors that fall out of that paradigm are high verbosity

insights.claim: Aristotle frames its core engine as 'optimal next pedagogical action prediction' - choosing whether to speak, stay silent, highlight, draw on a whiteboard (a code sandbox generating diagrams in real time) or pose a new problem - rather than next-token text generation.
insights.speaker: Sean Ready (Aristotle)
insights.so_what: Defines the product moat as a decision policy over multimodal teaching actions, not a prompt wrapper.
insights.quote: the way that we frame the the engine here is we're predicting the next optimal pedagogical action

insights.claim: Aristotle is building its own harness plus what it calls the first internal benchmarks and evals defining good one-on-one human-to-AI instruction, noting even the learning-science literature lacks heuristics for good one-on-one instruction.
insights.speaker: Sean Ready (Aristotle)
insights.so_what: Proprietary evals in an under-specified domain can be a defensible asset versus big labs.
insights.quote: we are building our own internal set of benchmarks and eval which are the first of its kind

insights.claim: Aristotle has a team of tutors hand-grading thousands of hours of teaching sessions to create training data that Sean Ready says does not exist anywhere, and the company will not sell it because it is under-18 student data it commits to keep locked down.
insights.speaker: Sean Ready (Aristotle)
insights.so_what: Proprietary labeled tutoring data is a moat and an alternative asset (Jason suggests it would be valuable to data vendors like Micro One).
insights.quote: it does not exist, but we're not selling it. It's ours.

insights.claim: Aristotle is increasingly post-training separate models as constituents of its harness (math problem generation, whiteboard-state reading, student voice understanding) because the data is too sparse for a single generalized model to do everything.
insights.speaker: Sean Ready (Aristotle)
insights.so_what: Signals a compound-system architecture strategy for vertical AI rather than reliance on one frontier model.
insights.quote: It doesn't really make sense to have one generalized model.

insights.claim: Sean Ready claims no one besides Aristotle is working on a tutoring model or a frontier tutoring harness, and says well-capitalized labs are instead doing work that undermines American education.
insights.speaker: Sean Ready (Aristotle)
insights.so_what: Claims an uncontested niche; investors should test whether big labs or Khan Academy/Brilliant enter.
insights.quote: no one is working on a tutoring model. No one is really working on a frontier tutoring harness outside of Aristotle

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis notes vertical AI app companies fear frontier labs copying them (citing Cursor feeling Anthropic took its business, Figma vs Claude design) and that some have forked open-source models like DeepSeek or GLM rather than put data into frontier models.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Platform-risk from frontier labs is pushing vertical apps toward open-weight models and proprietary data.
insights.quote: cursor felt like anthropic stole their business

themes.theme: AI tutoring business model and market

insights.claim: Aristotle prices like a tutoring services business: about $50/month for eight sessions and an unlimited plan around $199-200/month, with some students using 60+ hours a month - roughly $600 to $2,400 per year per student.
insights.speaker: Sean Ready (Aristotle)
insights.so_what: Premium pricing anchored to human tutoring rather than SaaS edtech implies high ARPU if retention holds.
insights.quote: we have students that'll do 60 plus hours a month and that comes in at $200

insights.claim: Sean Ready says Aristotle deliberately spends heavily on tokens and multi-agent architecture for quality, arguing edtech has never pushed the technology frontier or 'token maxed' because education was not historically economically valuable for private companies.
insights.speaker: Sean Ready (Aristotle)
insights.so_what: Gross margins may be lower than Jason assumes; quality-over-cost is the explicit strategy.
insights.quote: People have not pushed the frontier on new technology and token maxing in education.

insights.claim: Most US tutoring demand comes from 13-18 year olds (AP, IB, SAT, ACT prep), which is Aristotle's current core market, though the stated vision is a tutor that teaches anything to anyone.
insights.speaker: Sean Ready (Aristotle)
insights.so_what: Defines the beachhead: test-prep-anxious parents with high willingness to pay.
insights.quote: Most demand for tutoring in the US comes from 13 to 18 year olds.

insights.claim: Dyslexic students and their parents have been a huge market for Aristotle, per its CEO.
insights.speaker: Sean Ready (Aristotle)
insights.so_what: Adaptive voice tutoring may find early product-market fit in learning-difference segments.
insights.quote: the dyslexic student market has been huge for us

insights.claim: Sean Ready cites Bloom's two sigma finding (one-on-one tutoring improves outcomes by two standard deviations) and says fewer than one in 52 US students has a personal tutor, framing AI as the first way to scale it.
insights.speaker: Sean Ready (Aristotle)
insights.so_what: Frames the TAM as the gap between proven tutoring efficacy and near-zero access.
insights.quote: less than one out of every 52 students in the US have a personal tutor

insights.claim: A parent told Aristotle their daughter felt she learned more in three hours with Aristotle than in the prior month of public school, and the company reports increasingly long sessions.
insights.speaker: Sean Ready (Aristotle)
insights.so_what: Engagement anecdote supporting retention; not quantified.
insights.quote: she's learned more in three hours with Aristotle than in the last month of public school

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis predicts that if Aristotle succeeds it will be dragged into classrooms and teacher dashboards, as happened with Khan Academy and Brilliant.org once students brought the tools to school.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Consumer-to-institution adoption path could open B2B school sales.

insights.claim: Sean Ready positions Aristotle for schools as a TA that knows how each student learns, and argues US per-student education spending has risen exponentially while outcomes fell, so AI will 'solve' curricula delivery and leave schools to focus on social, emotional and physical education.
insights.speaker: Sean Ready (Aristotle)
insights.so_what: Long-term thesis that the instruction layer of public education gets unbundled to AI.
insights.quote: we're spending more and more on worse product

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis argues Americans dislike data centers, billionaires and AI, and that the way to change sentiment is products that save money, make money, entertain or educate - with AI tutoring being the clearest upside for parents.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Education is a politically favorable AI category amid broad AI backlash.
insights.quote: Americans at this point in time hate data centers, billionaires, and AI generally speaking

themes.theme: AI doomerism as Frontier Lab marketing

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis says AI doomerism is driven by Frontier Labs who have learned that framing releases as dangerously powerful (e.g., able to hack systems) increases usage and token consumption - while they may also sincerely believe it.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Treat safety-themed launch narratives partly as demand generation.
insights.quote: every time they put a release out that their products are incredibly powerful and can hack a system, etc., their usage goes up

insights.claim: Lon Harris says a New York Times report that Anthropic privately consulted religious scholars on instilling morality and whether Claude has a soul shifted him from David Sacks' regulatory-capture view toward believing Anthropic staff sincerely think they are 'making God in a box'.
insights.speaker: Lon Harris
insights.so_what: Anthropic's behavior may be ideologically rather than purely commercially driven, affecting regulatory and product posture.
insights.quote: They're they're they think they're making God in a box

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis frames frontier-lab researchers as in an 'understandable psychosis' caused by watching capability curves go from doubling every three years to every three or four weeks, likening it to Manhattan Project scientists.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Explains why lab leadership behavior may diverge from commercial logic as capability acceleration perception rises.
insights.quote: It's an understandable psychosis.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis states his own view that AI is 'just software', even while steelmanning that if one believed silicon consciousness were possible, consulting theologians would be logical.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Prominent VC skepticism of AI consciousness narratives.
insights.quote: I do think it's just software.

themes.theme: Founder playbook: capital, customer discovery and corporate intelligence

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis argues $500K is too much money to start a company in 2026; founders need roughly $10-20K a month to cover costs and one employee, and more becomes a distraction since AI credits are often free.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Points to collapsing seed capital needs for AI-native startups, pressuring traditional seed round sizes.
insights.quote: Who needs 500 grand to start a company in 2026?

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis says that with $500K in 1996 he would have become an angel investor in technology - starting an email newsletter and placing bets - rather than only funding his own magazine.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Reinforces his view of newsletter-plus-angel-investing as a high-leverage path.
insights.quote: Hands down, I would have become an angel investor in the technology industry.

insights.claim: For a builder selling AI drug-discovery tools to pharma, Jason Calacanis says selling tools is far easier than going through FDA regulation, and advises customer discovery with people inside big companies, who rarely steal ideas; the real copycats are hungry founders in accelerators like Y Combinator, Techstars or Founder University.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Picks-and-shovels in AI biotech avoid regulatory timelines; competition risk comes from startups, not incumbents.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis describes 'dark arts' customer research: setting up a neutral-sounding research firm that pays professionals (e.g., $100 for a 30-minute call with CPAs) to compare the startup's product against competitors, similar to how Gartner shields corporate clients - while warning against inducing NDA breaches.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Low-cost competitive intelligence tactic that also builds a first-customer pipeline.
insights.quote: there are people who will set up a research fund firm, pay people to do calls

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis says AI agents (he cites Grokbot) can now find target buyers by title, identify contact routes and set up customer discovery calls.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Agentic outbound is compressing early sales and research costs.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis notes that AI is being used on the fringes of drug discovery, citing a man who used AI to help make a cancer vaccine for his dog, and frames the path as wild-west tinkerers to startups to acquisition or copying by big pharma.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Maps the exit path for AI-bio startups: acquisition by slow-moving pharma.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis advises finance students to be 'AI first': run their own AI agents as one-on-one tutors alongside coursework, and do ambitious independent projects such as modeling Kleiner Perkins' 1980s-90s fund returns (DPI, TVPI, 30-year IRR) had they held Apple and Cisco shares.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Signals what top VCs value in junior talent: AI-native, self-directed analytical work.
insights.quote: I'm waiting for some ambitious kid who does that while they're at school.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis says employees who work for entrepreneurs get put in narrow boxes, and that would-be founders should instead run small full-stack projects to learn every chore from taxes and NDAs to LLC formation and payroll.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Generalist operator skill is the founder-development thesis behind his internal newsletter experiments.
